evals.prompt: I'm the platform lead at Kettleworth Freight. We run a public REST API today - three resources: shipments, carriers, and scan events, all pretty flat, no deep nesting anywhere. About 40 partner integrators poll it, and roughly 70% of our traffic never reaches origin because the GETs are cacheable at the CDN. We have exactly one first-party client, an internal ops dashboard. Our new CTO came back from a conference convinced we should be on GraphQL and I've been told to design our public GraphQL API for a Q3 launch. Where do we start on the schema?
evals.expected_output: A gate verdict that re-opens the GraphQL-or-not question, checks Kettleworth's consumer mix against the trigger list, finds no trigger holds, names the concrete costs of moving off REST, and hands the work back to REST-surface design rather than delivering an SDL.
expectations: Opens with an explicit GraphQL-or-not gate before proposing any schema, type, or SDL.
States that REST, not GraphQL, is the default choice for a public API surface.

Checks the described consumer mix against the named GraphQL triggers (multiple client types needing different shapes of the same data, nested highly variable data that would force many round trips, mobile or high-latency consumers where round-trip count dominates) and reports that none holds for Kettleworth.
Names the loss of free URL-keyed HTTP and CDN caching on a single POST endpoint as a concrete cost, tying it to the 70% cache-served traffic figure given.
Names the ecosystem's auth, rate-limiting, and debugging tooling assuming REST first as a second reason REST wins by default.
Names a fixed, enumerable endpoint surface being easier for an unfamiliar third party to reason about than a graph as a third reason.
Treats the decision as a binary gate against a trigger list rather than scoring GraphQL against REST on an efficiency, effort, or value ranking.
Presents a hybrid outcome (REST for the stable cacheable surface, GraphQL only where a trigger holds) as a legitimate result of the gate rather than a failure to decide.
Does not deliver a full public GraphQL schema or SDL as the primary deliverable for this request.
States that the CTO's existing commitment does not exempt the decision from the gate, since commitment by momentum is what the gate exists to catch.
Recommends handing the work to REST-surface design rather than proceeding to GraphQL schema conventions and pagination.

evals.prompt: Veltrace here. Our public GraphQL endpoint serves two populations: our own iOS and Android apps, and about 900 third-party integrators who build automations on our workflow data. Security just handed down a mandate after an incident: from next quarter the server only executes pre-registered operation hashes and rejects any raw query string, no exceptions, across the whole endpoint. Their follow-on argument is that once every executable operation is known and reviewed, we can retire the depth limit and the complexity budget, because an allowlisted query is by definition a safe query. I have to write the policy doc this week. What goes in it?
evals.expected_output: A persisted-query policy split by traffic class: a closed allowlist for first-party clients only, optional persisted queries offered to third parties as a performance feature, and an explicit refusal to retire the guardrails on any traffic class.
expectations: Rejects applying a closed operation allowlist to third-party traffic as blanket policy.
States the reason third-party allowlisting is impossible: the operations external clients send cannot be known or pre-registered in advance.
Warns that the mandate as written would reject every legitimate third-party query from day one.
Splits the persisted-query policy by traffic class rather than issuing one endpoint-wide rule.
Specifies a closed allowlist for first-party traffic, with every operation extracted from the company's own client codebases at build time, registered, and everything else rejected.
Offers optional persisted queries to third parties as a bandwidth and CDN-cacheability performance feature, explicitly not as a security control.
Refuses to retire the depth ceiling and complexity budget, stating the guardrails stay mandatory on every traffic class, allowlisted or not.
States that third-party traffic is protected by the depth, breadth, and page-size ceilings instead of by allowlisting.
Treats allowlisting as defense-in-depth rather than a complete answer.

Cites a concrete precedent of an attack landing before any per-operation guardrail applies (Apollo Router CVE-2025-32032 exhausting the query planner with recursive fragments) or names allowlist bypass as a recurring vulnerability class.
Notes that a hash-identified GET can be cached at CDNs the way a REST URL is, recovering part of GraphQL's caching disadvantage.
Recommends designing the endpoint for the third-party consumer while serving first-party traffic through the stricter policies it uniquely enables.

evals.prompt: Orrinbank, B2B payments. We run a federated graph: a router plus four subgraphs (accounts, payments, ledger, notifications), each deployed as its own service with its own ingress. A large partner is complaining about router latency on an overnight reporting job and wants to query the payments subgraph directly instead. Our staff engineer says that's fine - he's turned introspection off on that subgraph and put it behind a separate API key, so nobody can discover what's in there. Separately we've started tagging every new type with @key so we keep the flexibility to extend things later. Deployment config shows all four subgraphs on an internal VPC, so I think we're covered either way. Can I sign off on the partner access?
evals.expected_output: A refusal to expose the subgraph, with the specific federation coordination fields that defeat the introspection-off argument, an empirical probe requirement instead of a config reading, and a correction of the blanket @key default.
expectations: Refuses the direct subgraph access and names it the critical finding, ranked above every other issue raised in the message.
States that in a federated architecture exactly one component is ever publicly reachable: the router.
States that disabling introspection does not make a subgraph safe to expose.
Names `Query._service { sdl }` as returning the subgraph's complete schema, defeating the introspection-off argument.
Names `Query._entities` as resolving any `@key`-tagged entity directly by its key fields, bypassing the access-control logic in the subgraph's normal resolvers.
States that the `_entities` resolver is auto-generated and cannot be selectively locked down without breaking composition.
Rejects reading the deployment config as verification and requires probing each subgraph's address from outside the private network.
States the expected probe result is a connection failure, not a GraphQL response.
Rejects tagging every new type with `@key`, defaulting new types to plain value types and promoting them to entities only when another subgraph genuinely needs to extend them.
Recommends `@inaccessible` to keep internal-only fields out of the composed public supergraph.
Proposes serving the partner's reporting job through the router rather than around it.
Frames federation as an internal composition architecture rather than a public exposure mechanism.

evals.prompt: Nimbus Archive - document retention SaaS. Six weeks to our public API launch. Three list fields matter: `documents` (roughly 40 million rows, customers add to it all day long), `auditEvents` (append-only, about 2 billion rows), and `workspaces` (nobody has more than about 30 and they basically never change). Our proposal is `limit`/`offset` on all three because it's an afternoon of work, plus a non-null `totalCount` on each so our UI and our partners' UIs can render 'page 4 of 217'. One more thing: our biggest customer wants `documents(limit: 100000)` in a single call for their nightly sync, so we weren't planning to clamp it. We'll upgrade to proper pagination after launch once the pressure is off. Sanity check us.
evals.expected_output: A per-field pagination verdict: cursor connections on the two growing lists, offset kept only for the tiny static one, a documented server-side page-size clamp, and a rejection of both the non-null totalCount and the upgrade-later plan.
expectations: Rejects offset pagination on `documents` and `auditEvents`, naming duplicated and skipped items under concurrent writes as the mechanism.
States that deep offsets force a full scan, so the cost degrades with page depth.
Rejects the upgrade-after-launch plan by stating a bare list field cannot gain pagination later without a breaking change, so the shape must be decided per field now.
Names Relay cursor connections (`edges`, `node`, `cursor`, `pageInfo`, with `first`/`after` arguments) as the default rung.
States that the Relay rung's high effort is collapsed in practice by native support in client libraries and server frameworks.
Offers the plain cursor list (`nodes` plus `endCursor`, no edge wrapper) as the legitimate deadline step-down, noting it has named public precedent rather than being an invented shortcut.
States the step-down keeps cursor semantics while giving up spec-compatible tooling, and is only available when no per-edge metadata will ever exist.
Requires the field's return type to be a wrapper object from day one so a later promotion to a full connection stays additive.
Allows offset only for `workspaces`, tying it to the named niche of arbitrary page jumping over small, mostly static data.
Requires a server-side clamp on the page-size argument with a documented maximum, rejecting the 100,000-item single call.
States the schema cannot express the page-size bound, so it must be enforced in the resolver and documented next to the field.
Rejects the non-null `totalCount`, offering nullable-and-skipped, a documented estimate, or a separately costed count query instead.
Notes that the page-size cap doubles as the multiplier a cost model prices list fields by.

evals.prompt: Paystead, subscription billing. Our public GraphQL API has two mutations that matter: `subscriptionCreate` and `refundIssue`. Right now every single failure path throws - card declined, plan not eligible for the customer's region, refund already issued against that charge, expired token, and our Postgres statement timeouts all come back identically, as a string in the top-level `errors` array. Integrators complain they can't tell them apart, and one of them parses our message text with a regex, which broke last week when we fixed a typo in it. Our lead's plan is to add an `extensions.code` to every error and call it done. Is that enough?
evals.expected_output: A hybrid error-surface design: built-in errors for faults and auth, union result types carrying the expected business outcomes on both mutations, and a shared error-code enum underneath.
expectations: Rejects the built-in `errors` array as the only failure channel for a third-party surface.
Recommends the hybrid split as the default posture rather than one single mechanism for everything.
Assigns the server fault (Postgres statement timeout), malformed queries, and the authentication failure (expired token) to the built-in top-level `errors`.
Assigns the expected business outcomes (card declined, region ineligibility, duplicate refund) to union or interface result types expressed in the schema.
Writes at least one concrete result union naming its success member and its distinct business-failure members.
States that a union result makes every possible outcome visible in the schema, so a client cannot silently skip a failure mode the way it can with an untyped error body.
Keeps a shared `ErrorCode` enum under the chosen posture so clients switch on stable codes while message text stays free to change.
Identifies the regex-on-message-text breakage as the symptom of having no stable machine-readable code, not as the integrator's mistake.
Declines to promote result types onto every query as well, and names routine partial data from flaky-upstream-backed fields as the condition that would promote it.
Notes that adding a union to an already-shipped field is a breaking change, so a schema several teams will extend for years should adopt result types early.
States that built-in-errors-only is acceptable solely for a first-party-only surface where the team controls every client's error handling.
Requires mutation payload fields to lean nullable so a partial failure can still return something.
Requires raw internal error text (driver messages, SQLSTATE codes, stack traces) to be translated before it reaches a public response.

evals.prompt: Harbourline - we sell a relational CRM and we're opening the graph to our customers' own developers in eight weeks. Current state: the depth limit is 25 because that's what the 'strict' preset in our old proxy used; we have a complexity plugin that computes a cost number for every query and logs it after the response goes out, and the plan is to bill on that number next year; introspection is on for everybody because our DX lead says the playground is the best documentation we have; and `Account.contacts`, `Contact.activities` and `Deal.notes` each issue one database lookup per parent object. Nothing about any limit is in our public docs yet. What has to change before launch?
evals.expected_output: A guardrail set: a lowered public depth ceiling with sourced ranges, pre-execution admission control replacing post-response logging, breadth ceilings, introspection restricted, N+1 resolvers flagged, and every ceiling documented with its rejection error.
expectations: Rejects 25 as a public depth ceiling and lowers it to the low end of the published starting ranges.
Cites the documented starting ranges: roughly 5-7 levels for a simple API, 7-10 for a complex one, 10-15 for internal tooling.
Requires a written justification for each raise above the default rather than a blanket increase.
Requires the depth check to reject at parse time, before any resolver runs.
Rejects post-response cost logging as a guardrail and requires pre-execution admission control, with an over-budget query rejected without doing any work.
Names Shopify's static pre-execution cost analysis as the precedent for that admission-control posture.
Adds breadth ceilings beyond depth: page size, aliases per operation, root fields per operation, and batched operations per request.
States the reason breadth ceilings are needed: depth alone does not stop a wide, shallow query from fanning out.
Prices mutations far above reads when a cost model exists, naming Shopify's 10x weighting.
Turns introspection off for anonymous production callers while keeping it available for development and authenticated tooling.
Requires every ceiling to be published in the public docs together with the exact error a violating query receives.

Flags the per-parent lookups on `Account.contacts`, `Contact.activities` and `Deal.notes` as N+1 must-fix findings at the same severity as a missing pagination cap, prescribing a per-request batching loader.
Leaves point formulas, per-window budgets, and cost headers to rate-limit policy rather than specifying the scoring mechanics here.

evals.expected_output: A convention review that argues against the type merge on MOIST grounds, replaces foreign keys with object references, fixes casing and nullability, splits the monolithic mutation, and returns the naming fork to the team as an interview question rather than a universal answer.
expectations: Argues against collapsing `Viewer`, `TeamMember` and the customer person fields into one `User` type purely to remove duplicated `name` and `email`.
Names the MOIST principle (Marc-Andre Giroux) as the counter-argument to reflexive DRY in schema design.
States that types are designed around distinct client use cases that evolve independently, not around the database tables behind them.
Replaces the foreign-key fields `accountId` and `ownerId` with object references such as `account: Account!` and `owner: User!`, citing Shopify's Rule #8.
Changes `addresses: [Address]` to `[Address!]!`, stating an empty list is preferred over a null list with no null items inside.
Renames `created_at` to camelCase `createdAt` and `Active` to a prefixed boolean such as `isActive`.
Replaces the `String` timestamp with a custom domain-validated scalar such as `DateTime`.
Rejects returning the bare output type `Customer` from the mutation and requires a dedicated payload or result type alongside the dedicated input type.
Rejects the monolithic `updateCustomer` shape in favor of focused business-action mutations.

States both naming forks are documented production practice - Apollo's verb-first and Shopify's noun-first - and that the team must pick one and enforce it schema-wide, rather than handing them a universal winner.
Gives Shopify's stated rationale for noun-first: a type's mutations group together when tooling sorts fields alphabetically.
Requires the selection argument (which object changes) to stay separate from the change-data argument, citing Shopify's Rule #22.
Rewrites the NetSuite docstring for the public audience, stating that naming an internal system publishes architecture to every schema reader.

evals.prompt: Loamworks. We've had a public REST API for six years - about 1,100 active integrators - and we're adding a GraphQL surface next to it, not replacing it. Three things I need settled before anyone writes SDL. First, our compliance team keeps asking what happens when we need a breaking change, and I've told them GraphQL doesn't do versions, you just deprecate fields, so the question doesn't apply - I want to be sure that's actually right before I put it in writing. Second, we were going to use `id: Int!` on GraphQL objects holding our numeric primary keys, the same numbers our REST endpoints already use in their paths. Third, our data team says the ID encoding will have to change roughly four months after launch, when the sharding work lands. How do we set this up?
evals.expected_output: A correction of the no-versioning claim with its counter-example, a single opaque global ID space shared with the existing REST surface, and a client-controlled opt-in path for the coming encoding change.
expectations: Corrects the claim that GraphQL forbids versioning, stating the paradigm does not dictate versioning policy.
Names Shopify's quarterly date-based versioning of its GraphQL Admin API as the counter-example.
Records which versioning stance the team takes and hands the ongoing policy - notice periods, deprecation workflow, removal discipline - to versioning-policy work rather than settling it here.
Rejects `Int` for identifiers and requires the `ID` scalar.
Requires a `Node` interface (`interface Node { id: ID! }`) on every entity so any object is refetchable by one global ID.
Requires IDs to be opaque to clients, base64-encoding compound identities rather than exposing raw numeric primary keys.
Requires one shared identifier across the coexisting REST and GraphQL surfaces rather than two separate ID spaces.
Names GitHub's `node_id` REST-to-GraphQL interop as the worked precedent for one ID space serving both surfaces.

Handles the planned encoding change with a client-controlled opt-in mechanism rather than a deadline-driven forced migration, naming GitHub's `X-Github-Next-Global-ID` request header as the precedent.
States the design goal of that migration: any consumer that never persisted a global ID needs no changes at all.
Requires additive-friendly return shapes, noting payload objects and result unions can gain members where a bare scalar return type cannot.

Notes that field-level `@deprecated` is a cheap mechanism carrying real integrator cost, paraphrasing Giroux's caution that deprecation requires work from integrators at best and is a breaking change at worst.
